metadata.summary: Diagnose the recent-jaundice syndrome, evaluate competing causes, distinguish confidence from severity, and coordinate urgent care.
metadata.application: Explain why a presentation supports probable or possible AH, identify the remaining differential, and decide whether selective confirmation would change management.
keyPoints: An AST:ALT ratio supports AH but does not prove it.
Biopsy is selective when diagnostic uncertainty matters.
Severity assessment follows diagnosis and does not establish the cause.

bodies.heading: Recognize the acute clinical syndrome
bodies.body: Alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH) is a clinical syndrome of recent onset or worsening jaundice in a person with a compatible history of heavy alcohol exposure. It differs from alcohol-related steatosis and from the chronic structural changes of cirrhosis, although these conditions can coexist. Established cirrhosis or every feature of decompensation is not required for AH. First establish the time course and evaluate the patient, rather than assigning the diagnosis from the presence of alcohol use alone.

bodies.heading: Reconstruct the exposure and jaundice timeline
bodies.body: Ask respectfully about the amount and duration of alcohol use, the last drink and the onset of jaundice. The 2024 ACG guideline Table 5 describes probable AH using recent jaundice within 60 days of heavy use, more than 50 g of alcohol per day for at least six months, the compatible laboratory pattern and no other cause of acute hepatitis. Earlier AASLD guidance describes the original consensus exposure thresholds as more than 40 g/day for women or 60 g/day for men, with less than 60 days of abstinence before jaundice. Identify the definition being applied rather than blending these criteria. These diagnostic criteria do not define a safe amount of alcohol for a person with liver disease. An uncertain exposure history lowers diagnostic confidence and deserves further evaluation.

bodies.heading: Interpret the pattern and its limitations
bodies.body: The ACG probable-AH pattern includes bilirubin greater than 3 mg/dL, AST 50 to 400 U/L and an AST:ALT ratio greater than 1.5. Worked example: AST 180 U/L and ALT 90 U/L give 180 ÷ 90 = 2, a supportive ratio. With recent jaundice, bilirubin 6 mg/dL, compatible exposure and no competing cause, this supports probable AH. The ratio alone does not prove the diagnosis. AST and ALT reflect injury; bilirubin, INR, albumin and the clinical course provide different information about liver function and illness. Markedly atypical aminotransferases, such as values in the thousands, require evaluation for alternative or additional causes rather than an automatic AH label.

bodies.heading: Actively evaluate competing causes
bodies.body: Review prescribed drugs, recent changes, nonprescription medicines, supplements and toxins. Evaluate viral hepatitis, biliary obstruction, ischemic injury and autoimmune disease when indicated by the history, examination and investigations. Consider other vascular or metabolic causes in the appropriate context. Recent shock or a temporally plausible drug exposure can confound the diagnosis; neither alcohol history nor an abnormal ratio removes that possibility. Obtain indicated laboratory testing and imaging, and document which alternatives have been assessed and which remain unresolved.

bodies.heading: Search for infection and acute complications
bodies.body: AH can produce systemic inflammatory features without infection, and infection can also coexist. Leukocytosis, tachycardia or a negative initial culture does not settle that distinction. Examine for infection sources and obtain indicated cultures, imaging and other investigations while reassessing the patient. Cirrhosis with ascites requires particular attention: new AKI, confusion or an emergent admission may warrant prompt diagnostic paracentesis even without fever. Address bleeding, encephalopathy, kidney injury, unstable circulation and poor intake urgently. Do not postpone necessary treatment of a strongly suspected infection in an unstable patient while waiting for every result.

bodies.heading: Assign confidence and use biopsy selectively
bodies.body: Probable AH is a compatible clinical syndrome without a major diagnostic confounder. Possible AH has an uncertain exposure history, atypical findings or another plausible cause that limits confidence. Definite AH adds compatible histologic confirmation to the clinical diagnosis. A classic presentation without confounders does not require routine liver biopsy. When uncertainty persists and confirmation could change a treatment decision, discuss selective biopsy with hepatology; the ACG algorithm uses transjugular biopsy in this setting. Biopsy is part of clinical correlation and does not replace the exposure history or the assessment of competing causes.

bodies.heading: Assess severity after establishing the syndrome
bodies.body: Diagnostic confidence and severity answer different questions. The 2024 ACG guideline classifies AH as severe with an original MELD score greater than 20 and moderate at 20 or below. A supplied original MELD of 21 therefore falls in the severe group; 20 does not cross that threshold. Confirm the score version and the correct laboratory units instead of treating MELD, MELD-Na and other versions as automatically interchangeable. A severity score does not establish the cause of hepatitis or make corticosteroids automatically appropriate. Severe AH requires assessment of contraindications, infection and organ function before the liver team selects disease-directed therapy.

bodies.heading: Communicate a coordinated initial plan
bodies.body: A useful handoff states the jaundice and exposure timeline, laboratory pattern, diagnostic confidence, competing causes, severity and urgent complications. Arrange nutrition assessment, indicated supplementation and alcohol use disorder treatment alongside the acute liver evaluation. Continue serial assessment of mental status, circulation, kidney function, electrolytes, liver trajectory and intake. Uncertainty about the final cause does not suspend supportive care or treatment of acute complications. Recovery follow-up should include hepatology, nutrition and a concrete alcohol cessation and AUD care plan.

check.question: In a patient being evaluated for AH, AST falls while INR rises and kidney function worsens. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
choices: Reassess liver function, organ deterioration and complications; a falling injury marker alone does not establish recovery.
Declare recovery solely because AST has fallen.
Disregard kidney function because it is unrelated to severity assessment.
Use the AST decline to exclude every competing cause of hepatitis.
check.rationale: AST is an injury marker and its trajectory cannot independently establish recovery. INR, kidney function and the clinical course provide separate information relevant to function and severity. Worsening organ function warrants prompt reassessment of complications and competing causes. Neither the AST trend nor one isolated laboratory result excludes the differential.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-069.question: A man reports 80 g of alcohol daily for two years, last used two weeks ago. Jaundice began one week ago. Bilirubin is 6 mg/dL, AST 180 U/L and ALT 90 U/L; evaluation identifies no competing acute cause. Which assessment best fits the 2024 ACG criteria?
choices: Probable AH based on the compatible clinical syndrome, without mandatory routine biopsy.
Definite AH established by the AST:ALT ratio alone.
AH is excluded because cirrhosis has not already been proven.
AH requires bilirubin below 3 mg/dL.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-069.rationale: The exposure and recent-jaundice timeline, bilirubin above 3 mg/dL, AST 50 to 400 U/L, ratio 180/90 = 2 and absence of a competing cause support probable AH. Histologic confirmation would be needed for the definite category; the ratio alone does not establish it. Established cirrhosis is not a prerequisite, and a bilirubin below 3 mg/dL does not match this probable-AH criterion.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-070.question: AST is 180 U/L and ALT 90 U/L, but the jaundice timeline and alcohol exposure history have not been obtained. What can the laboratory ratio establish at this stage?
choices: The ratio is 2 and can support a compatible pattern, but cannot establish AH by itself.
The ratio is 0.5 and proves AH independently of history.
The ratio is 2 and eliminates the need to assess competing causes.
The ratio is 270 and establishes definite AH without biopsy.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-070.rationale: Dividing AST by ALT gives 180/90 = 2. A ratio above 1.5 is one component of the ACG probable-AH pattern, interpreted with jaundice, exposure, bilirubin, AST range and the differential. It does not independently establish the clinical syndrome or exclude alternatives. Addition of the enzyme values is not the ratio.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-071.question: A patient with heavy alcohol exposure develops jaundice after circulatory shock. AST is 2,500 U/L and ALT 2,200 U/L. What is the best diagnostic approach?
choices: Evaluate ischemic injury and other competing or additional causes before assigning AH as the explanation.
Diagnose probable AH solely because heavy alcohol exposure is present.
Treat the markedly elevated enzymes as the typical ACG probable-AH pattern.
Exclude all additional causes whenever jaundice follows alcohol exposure.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-071.rationale: Shock is an important diagnostic confounder, and enzymes in the thousands are outside the ACG probable-AH AST pattern of 50 to 400 U/L. Evaluate ischemic injury and other alternatives rather than attributing the presentation to alcohol history alone. This does not assert that coexisting alcohol-related disease is impossible.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-072.question: A jaundiced patient reports heavy alcohol use and recently started a potentially hepatotoxic medicine. The cause remains uncertain. Which next step best protects diagnostic accuracy?
choices: Review the medication and supplement timeline and investigate drug-related and other competing causes.
Declare definite drug-induced injury solely because a new medicine was started.
Ignore the new exposure because heavy alcohol use proves AH.
Use the AST:ALT ratio to exclude all medication-related injury.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-072.rationale: A temporally plausible medication exposure can confound an AH diagnosis and warrants a careful timeline and differential. Neither the new medicine alone nor alcohol history alone proves the cause. The AST:ALT ratio does not exclude drug-related injury; further clinical evaluation determines confidence and management.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-073.question: A compatible AH clinical syndrome is supported by a liver biopsy interpreted with the exposure history and competing-cause evaluation. Which diagnostic-confidence category applies?
choices: Definite AH with compatible histologic confirmation.
Possible AH solely because a biopsy was performed.
Probable AH is the only category that permits any histology.
Definite AH requires no compatible clinical syndrome.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-073.rationale: In the guidance framework, definite AH combines the compatible clinical diagnosis with histologic confirmation. Probable AH is a compatible clinical syndrome without important confounders and without requiring biopsy. Possible AH reflects uncertainty or confounding. Histology still requires clinical correlation; it does not erase the need for the history and differential.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-074.question: A patient has new jaundice but an uncertain alcohol exposure history and another plausible cause of hepatitis. The choice of disease-directed treatment depends on the cause after initial evaluation. Which plan is best?
choices: Discuss selective biopsy with hepatology if confirmation could change management, while continuing urgent complication care.
Automatically give corticosteroids because any jaundice establishes severe AH.
Require biopsy in every classic AH presentation before evaluating infection.
Abandon evaluation of the competing cause because AH is always histologically obvious.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-074.rationale: Uncertain exposure or a plausible alternative cause fits possible AH. If diagnostic confirmation will affect treatment, guidance supports selective biopsy with the liver team; the ACG algorithm describes the transjugular route. Biopsy is not mandatory for every classic unconfounded presentation, and diagnostic work should proceed alongside urgent supportive and complication care.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-075.question: A patient has a compatible AH diagnosis and a correctly calculated original MELD score of 21. Which statement matches the 2024 ACG severity framework?
choices: The score is above the severe-AH threshold of 20; treatment still requires assessment of eligibility and complications.
A score of 21 is moderate because severe AH requires a score above 32.
The score itself establishes alcohol as the cause of hepatitis.
The score guarantees that corticosteroids are appropriate without further assessment.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-075.rationale: ACG classifies AH as severe with original MELD greater than 20; a score of 20 or below is moderate in this framework. The historic modified discriminant-function threshold of 32 should not be substituted as a MELD threshold. Severity does not prove etiology or remove the need to assess infection, contraindications and organ function before disease-directed therapy.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-076.question: During an AH evaluation, a patient has leukocytosis and tachycardia. Initial cultures are negative. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
choices: AH can cause systemic inflammation without infection, but infection may coexist and still requires clinical source evaluation.
Leukocytosis proves infection, regardless of the rest of the evaluation.
Negative initial cultures rule out every infection source and end surveillance.
AH excludes infection, so evaluating both is unnecessary.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-076.rationale: Systemic inflammatory features can occur in AH without infection, and infection may coexist. Leukocytosis and tachycardia are not independently diagnostic of infection; negative initial cultures also do not end the clinical assessment. Continue indicated source evaluation, surveillance and treatment when clinically warranted.
